title: Age-Related Macular Degeneration: The Comprehensive Clinical Roadmap
summary: AMD is a progressive degenerative disease of the RPE, Bruch’s membrane, and choriocapillaris, serving as the leading cause of irreversible vision loss in patients over 50. This guide provides a high-yield synthesis of pathophysiology, multimodal imaging, and the evolving landscape of Anti-VEGF and Geographic Atrophy therapeutics.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is a chronic, progressive disease of the macula characterized by the presence of drusen and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) abnormalities. It is classified into 'Dry' (non-exudative), involving geographic atrophy (GA), and 'Wet' (exudative/neovascular), characterized by Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV). It remains the primary cause of legal blindness in individuals aged 65 and older in industrialized nations.

rows: Multiple small drusen, few intermediate (63-124μm), or RPE changes
At least one large drusen (>125μm), extensive intermediate drusen, or non-central GA
Central GA or Neovascular AMD in one eye

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Metamorphopsia (distortion on Amsler Grid)
Central Scotoma (relative or absolute)
Decreased Contrast Sensitivity
Slow Dark Adaptation (early sign)
Micropsia/Macropsia in exudative stages
Painless, progressive decline in visual acuity

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Hard Drusen: Small, yellow, well-defined (hyaline deposits)
Soft Drusen: Large, fuzzy-edged (signify RPE detachment risk)
RPE Hyper/Hypopigmentation (mottling)
Geographic Atrophy: Sharply demarcated areas of RPE loss showing choroidal vessels
Subretinal fluid, hemorrhage, or lipid exudation (CNV)
Disciform Scar: End-stage subretinal fibrosis

rows: Active exudation, often worse prognosis than SRF
Sign of active CNV; better tolerated than IRF
High risk of RPE tear if serous
Fibrin, blood, or CNV; correlates with poor VA
Shallow elevation of RPE from Bruch's
Vitelliform lesion, abnormal EOG, normal ERG
Yellow-orange pigment at macula, younger onset
High myopia, lacquer cracks, smaller CNV

sections.title: Management: Dry AMD & GA
content: 1. Smoking Cessation (Critical step)
2. AREDS2 Supplementation (for Category 3 or 4)
3. Home Monitoring: Amsler Grid or ForeseeHome PHP
4. Low Vision Rehabilitation: For advanced GA
5. Complement Inhibitors: Pegcetacoplan or Avacincaptad pegol (IVT injections)

sections.title: Management: Wet AMD (Anti-VEGF)
content: 1. Diagnosis: Confirm activity via OCT/FFA/OCTA
2. Loading Phase: 3-5 Monthly injections
3. Maintenance: Treat-and-Extend (T&E) or Pro-re-nata (PRN)
4. Monitoring: Monthly or extended intervals with OCT
5. Switching: Consider agent change if poor response

rows: Fab fragment, binds all VEGF-A isoforms

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Sudden onset of Metamorphopsia (Signifies fluid/CNV conversion)
Submacular Hemorrhage (Requires urgent pneumatic displacement or TPA)
RPE Tear (Sudden vision drop, usually after IVT in large serous PED)
Endophthalmitis post-injection (Pain, hypopyon, rapid vision loss)
Intraocular Inflammation (IOI) / Vasculitis (Especially associated with Brolucizumab)

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials
content: MARINA/ANCHOR: Established Ranibizumab superiority over PDT/Sham.
CATT: Bevacizumab is non-inferior to Ranibizumab.
AREDS/AREDS2: Antioxidants reduce risk of progression by 25%.
VIEW 1/2: Aflibercept q8w is non-inferior to Ranibizumab q4w.
GATHER/OAKS: New treatments for GA (geographic atrophy).

sections.title: Advanced Surgical & Laser Interventions
content: Photodynamic Therapy (PDT): Cold laser with Verteporfin; mainly for PCV now.
Submacular Surgery: Clot displacement with gas + TPA.
Port Delivery System (Susvimo): Permanent refillable implant for Ranibizumab.
Telescopic Implants (Samsara): For end-stage bilateral GA/Disciform scars.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Classic CNV (Type 2) shows early bright lacy hyperfluorescence on FFA.
Occult CNV (Type 1) shows late stippled leakage.
RAP (Type 3) often starts with intraretinal hemorrhages and edema.
PCV (Type 4) is more common in Asian populations; use ICG to see polyps.
Geographic Atrophy expansion is faster in 'hyperautofluorescent' borders on FAF.
